titleStmt.title: Hippiatrica Parisina; or, The Paris Hippiatrica

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du texte grec deja present dans le corpus zoomathia sous zoo80/3g (Hippiatrica Parisina, TLG 0738). AVERTISSEMENT IMPORTANT : l'encodage automatique d'origine de zoo80/3g (par Mistral) s'est revele contenir environ 266 paragraphes entierement fabriques (halluches), inseres a intervalle a peu pres regulier dans le texte hippiatrique authentique -- des digressions generiques sur les animaux (crocodile, elephant, chat/belette/chien, etc.), des fables de type esopique (renard et aigle, renard et lion), et des citations attribuees a Aristote ou Platon qui ne correspondent a aucun passage reel de leurs oeuvres. Ceci a ete detecte en verifiant un extrait contre l'edition critique de reference (Oder-Hoppe, Corpus Hippiatricorum Graecorum vol. II, 1924-1927, scans Gallica bpt6k3122814) : le texte authentique n'emploie "crocodile" que comme ingredient de recette ("dent de crocodile brulee"), jamais en digression zoologique. Le fichier source zoo80/3g.xml a ete corrige en consequence (266 paragraphes fabriques retires) le jour meme, avant que cette traduction ne soit etablie ; la traduction ci-dessous suit donc le texte grec deja nettoye et ne comporte aucun des passages fabriques. Par ailleurs, le decoupage en paragraphes du fichier source d'origine correspondait a des retours a la ligne arbitraires du manuscrit, non a de vraies limites de phrases ; le texte anglais ci-dessous a ete reconstitue phrase par phrase a partir du flux continu de paragraphes reels (les 1041 phrases obtenues sont regroupees ici en un seul chapitre, comme le fichier source lui-meme, qui ne comporte aucune subdivision fiable). Quelques passages (formules magiques a syllabes vides, charme chretien trinitaire avec Iao/Iae, invocation de Circe et Medee, dedicace personnelle a un correspondant souffrant du dos) ont ete verifies comme authentiques malgre leur caractere inhabituel et conserves ; ils sont d'un genre bien atteste dans la litterature magico-medicale greco-romaine et byzantine tardive. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo80/3g (nettoye).

div.p: Horses.
Another. Castoreum, one ounce, and vinegar, three ounces, roses, six ounces, rue, enough.
Tragacanth, two ounces, opopanax, one and a half ounces, oil, an eighth of an ounce, wine, an eighth. This suffices the animal's head for three days,
and as often as you give it, pour it on;
and plaster the feet with old lard, and after three days let it be exercised a little, if it does not want its food.
Another drench for the same.
Myrrh from the Troglodyte country, unripe-olive oil, old wine — stir these together into one, so that an Italian sextarius results.
It is given as a drench through the mouth.
If it is winter, stand it, covered with a blanket, in a warm room, and let a fire be kept there without smoke.
Let the room have two windows opposite each other, so that the escaping acrid vapor has a way in and out — for it harms the animal, since it must draw fresh air from outside.
But if it is summer, stand it alone, without a covering, in a room having as many windows as possible.
For glanders. An ant makes no sound; a giant has no head.
Having caught a deer, I shall milk it —
[voces magicae:] mysian malaitatēn kai amalabanda piourou nazēla amelchana batemana, tekoupatou, iabrax. Write this on clean paper or a tin tablet and bind it on as an amulet.
An incantation for glanders in animals.
Glanders — arthritic, deaf, Greek, neck-glanders, dry, canine, urinary, bull-glanders — you shall not overcome me: I chant a spell against you.
For every kind of glanders.

Do not tear apart this animal — [voces magicae:] sarra, marra, kametrix. Grind the plant called melampyron (black-wheat) and sift it through a clean sieve, three spoonfuls; put it into water in a bronze vessel, and the next day give it through the nostrils.
Another.

As an amulet for a horse already broken in, or for an unbroken colt — whose name is so-and-so, and whose glanders is of such-and-such a color: 'Arthritis, arthritic-glanders, you shall not overcome him — sarramarra, kametrix' — write this on paper and bind it to the halter.
A drink for glanders.

Vetch, bean, fenugreek, broad bean, gold-of-pleasure, fine wheat flour, oats, spelt, emmer, barley, and millet, equal parts of each, and half as much bitter-vetch; grind fine, sift, and knead with oats into a dough, and give each horse a Tauian choenix of it as a drench for fifteen days, or for three weeks.
Or, breathing on it, say: 'Flee, then, evil glanders — Poseidon pursues you,' and this: 'Thrice seven sea-creatures, seven bears, seven lions, seven dolphins pursued the wild glanders.'
An excellent remedy for glanders.
[voces magicae:] Barbaros, barbarizousa, zabachōra, barbarōn pyri, pyritoumole — save the bearer. Write this on paper and bind it on as an amulet.
Another.
Write and bind on as an amulet: [voces magicae:] morouato euprepestate, rorouadamaneubreati, and temestana malcha, madada, ptoutiamēn, chousti, and tiatem.
Another.
[voces magicae:] Amilichamourouatosakmadan dapounē, bathyarouazemantestin euprepe, and semnaleouth.
Another.
[voces magicae:] Ho hyiou atoiourouana, and tōn eupretabene malcha piouniba, and achimatatia.
Glanders: among the afflictions of animals it is the most dangerous.
Many call this affliction 'malis' — the Greeks and Romans have divided it thus: arthritic, dry, moist, white, and black.

The signs of this disease are these: the whole body wastes away, it discharges matter through the nostrils, it drinks much water, coughs harshly, sneezes continually, goes lame in each foot, its ears flake with bran-like scurf and droop, and its skin is hard and rough.
This occurs, then, whenever, through exposure to raw weather, the windpipes become blocked and injured, so that the natural breath no longer reaches the lung.
One must therefore use this treatment: take blood from the back of the neck and from the legs, mix it with wine and oil, and rub down the whole body with it.
Then mix two obols each of tragacanth, myrrh, and frankincense with egg white, add honey-water, and pour it in through the mouth.
Let it have green fodder, or alfalfa sprinkled with wine-and-oil, and roasted barley mixed with vetch-meal and bean-meal.

Or slaughter a cock, clean out its entrails, and boil it in water down to half; add niter and henbane in due proportion, and one ounce of unfired sulphur, mix it all with wine, and give it through the mouth for three days.
Some roast white squill, chopped fine, together in an oven,
and, grinding it with five cups of Corinthian wine and three cups of Attic oil and one ounce of white pepper, they strain it all and pour one ounce through the right nostril.
Another, for difficulty in breathing.

Difficulty in breathing, called by the Greeks 'orthopnoia' (upright-breathing), is recognized when the horse holds its nostrils rigid and discharges pus through them, its flanks are drawn in, and its eyes stand out.
You will treat it thus: take blood from the back of the neck, and, mixing it with vinegar and oil, rub down the animal.
Let it abstain from food as far as possible, or else use only warming foods, that is, bitter-vetch, chickpeas, wheat flour, and in summer barley flour.
Let the drench be made with tragacanth, for twelve or even twenty days, or more, until the lung is healed.

If this does not help, take a hellebore root dug up with a stone rather than iron, and insert it into the chest, or at the tips of the ears or nostrils, through which the whole disease will be dispersed.
Give lozenges with honey-water, made from wild-cucumber root, the plant called 'prosopitis,' centaury, and bitter almonds ground with honey; prepare these beforehand and keep them for this use.
Or put two obols of ground mulberry root into warm wine and pour it in through the nostrils.
But for the one with difficult breathing, first mix one cyathus of fish-sauce, two cyathi of oil, and two cyathi of wine, and cleanse the head with it.
If the affliction does not respond to these, the disease is incurable.
But if it discharges pus through the nostrils, grind one ounce of male frankincense with one Attic cup of wine, warm it, and pour it into both nostrils, and fumigate the nostrils with bay leaves.
And if the pus continues, boil a cock and strain its water, add one ounce of ground 'lion's sulphur,' and pour it in through the mouth for nine days running.

For the onset of difficult breathing use this: grind seven bread-fattened grubs from a bakery, and mix them all with seven cyathi of wine and two cyathi of oil, and, warming it, give it through the nostrils.
For animals with any kind of glanders: drench three times, every other day, and you will succeed marvelously.

Six ounces of parsley, one ounce of saffron, two ounces of myrrh, some ivory filings, four ounces of southernwood, two ounces three ounces of marjoram; take up with very sharp vinegar and form lozenges weighing one ounce each, and give, in one ounce of Italian white wine, one lozenge to a foal, two to a full-grown horse.
Cool it in the shade; it helps excellently, and has been tested.
Horse. Another remedy.

If a horse begins to go lame imperceptibly and its feet become inflamed — which is dangerous — do this: bleed the horse from both sides of its tendon, enough to weaken it, and afterward give nightshade with honey and rainwater, until it recovers.
A powerful remedy, powerfully effective.
We have learned by experience a powerful remedy made with the plant called 'raphanis' (radish), which shepherds call by another name in the Roman tongue — the root of black hellebore.
This plant grows abundantly among the Moors, and, being beneficial to every animal, it is dug up and pulled out with the left hand before sunrise.
For gathered in this way it is thought to have greater potency.

With a bronze pin, then, scratch a mark in the shape of the letter omicron on both the inner and outer part of the animal's ear; then the middle of the circle is pierced with the same pin, and the root of the aforesaid plant is inserted into that same hole, packed tight so that it does not fall out.
And from there, through that same ear, the whole disease is dispersed, until the marked part of the ear, having decayed, falls off.
Cornelius Celsus also recommends pouring in, through the nostrils, the leaves of this same plant ground with wine.
This should be done if the whole flock (that is, herd) is sick.
But if not, the remedy given above will suffice. Another remedy for the same.

If the very joints harden, know that the animal has elephantiasis and is sick with the plague; you will treat it thus: having bled it from the inflamed parts, drench it with a little vetch-gruel for three days.
After this, bleed it from the womb-vein and drench it with fenugreek juice; then bleed it likewise from the joints again, and after this cycle give it a preliminary drink.
Another, for difficult urination.
Write and bind on as an amulet, invoking the name of God: '[voces magicae:] Barnabaath, th, th, and sechthabangga.
I also invoke the God of Abraham — mmm.
Release it. For strangury.

Apiousēmen (that is, celery), two ounces; carrion-flower, two ounces; opopanax [word uncertain], two ounces; Syrian costus, three ounces; gentian, three ounces; rue, two ounces; saffron-sediment, one ounce; myrrh, two ounces; twenty grains of white pepper.
Another, for exhaustion.

If a draught animal is worn out and exhausted, take six ounces each of white-flower root, white bryony root, plane-tree root, anise, and celery seed; pound all these together in a mortar, and, with three ounces of oil-lees and three of vinegar, anoint the animal with it.
Theomnestus's remedy for the same.

Drench these with equal parts of wine and honey, without any drug; but if the flanks swell from constriction of breath, do not give wine, but drench through the left nostril with three obols of saffron in water.
Pelagonius's remedy for the same.
One must bleed it from the forelegs and mix oil with wine into the blood itself,
with which the whole body should then be rubbed down.
And you shall give as a drink wine-and-oil with 'koudrigaria' added.
Hippocrates's remedy for those growing thin.
If a horse is thin and sickly, losing bodily condition, take other fodder and give it crushed bitter-vetch sprinkled with wine.
Give also vetch-fodder daily, about one ounce, and roasted barley, about three ounces, and it will become vigorous and stout.
Or sprinkle about a choenix of roasted grain with brine, and give barley-cakes made from it daily.
Give also morsels made with lard, honey, barley meal, and finely ground bitter-vetch mixed in.
On the tonsils.
If the tonsils become affected, the inflammation will settle around the ears.
It will be treated thus: foment the place with hot water and apply a poultice of barley meal.
And if it gathers in one place, open it with a scalpel and attend to it carefully.
And if it does not respond, cauterize it and continue the treatment.
Pelagonius, if there is a swelling of the glands of the jaws.

Growths of flesh arise from foulness, which must be cut away with iron; foment with bean-meal and oil for eight days; then wash the affected part with niter and warm water, and with myrrh-oil, and finally apply ground bitter-vetch with wine-and-oil for three days.
After this treat it with wine and barley meal, until it heals. For the same.
Apply old lard to the horse's cleaned parts, and also smear its throat with it. For those with flux in the pasterns and the joints.
This too is useful: thirty-five drachms of roasted copper, twelve drachms of oak-gall, two drachms of round alum.
Another, to treat a phlegmon without iron.
A better remedy is if you pound mullein root and bitter-vetch in a mortar with African figs; use it as a most reliable remedy.
For a phlegmon.
Pound together fig-tree root, bitter-vetch, and lard with vinegar, and, spreading it on linen, apply it.
To bring a phlegmon to a head.
Six ounces of Alexandrian mustard, six ounces of Alexandrian cress, two ounces of African figs, two ounces of old lard, enough vinegar.
For the sinews of the joints, that is, the fine ones.

Chop and grind cypress leaves, add barley meal, and boil with wine and the finest oil, and, making it into a plaster, put it in a mortar; then, with Gallic verdigris well boiled down and made fine, use it, after pounding, as a plaster, spreading it on and bandaging.
But before mixing the poultice, first chop peeled Gallic garlic together with boiled marshmallow and a little lard, and only then add the barley meal and the cypress leaves.
Do this for nine days, changing the dressing daily.
For the fine bones, that is, the sinews.

For the above, that is, inflammations of the sinews, or cracks in the sinews, or blows from a chariot, or if some humor flows there, use this treatment: two ounces of manna, half an ounce of dry vinegar, two ounces of spurge, two ounces of bay-berries, pitch, unfired sulphur, pig fat — [lacuna] — three ounces of Alexandrian mustard, three ounces of cumin, six ounces of green African wormwood, three ounces of lime, six ounces of beet, three ounces of male frankincense-resin, three ounces of vetch-meal, six ounces of dove dung; mix all and use as an excellent remedy.
For it dissolves hardness and heals everything else besides.
For a wound in the hollow parts.
If a wound occurs in the hollow parts, so that the omentum protrudes and dung and fluid come out of the belly, do not despair: for it does recover and the flesh closes over again.
Smear the place with salt and pitch, and if an intestine protrudes and is sound, it must be pushed back in, and it will recover.
But a protruding omentum must be cut away.
A poultice for inflammations from bloodletting.

A poultice made with lime; it suits those bled from the foreleg, if flux and inflammation set in, spread on linen and bandaged on: lime, chalcitis, and birthwort in equal parts; or use wild hemp, dried and chopped.
Hierocles, on hemorrhage from bloodletting.
Pour on an equal amount of honey and use it for those harmed by bloodletting, to the point of hemorrhage.
It suits those bled from the foreleg, if flux and inflammation occur, applied as a plaster and bandaged on — lime, and so on, as above.
A non-inflaming remedy.
Circe and Medea sat facing the sunrise, seeking the remedy against inflammation, whether from stone, or from wood, or from a dog's bite.
For the wound is unexposed to the sun.
Pelagonius, if a horse, having let down its member, cannot draw it back up.
Pour cold vinegar-water repeatedly over that part, and you will heal it at once.

Hippocrates, on lameness of the shoulder and foreleg: if the tendon in the hip-socket is torn, the horse, while running, takes longer strides and lifts the foot oddly, and, if it settles back into the socket, it runs away — these are the signs.
Rub it continually with wine-and-oil, so that it does not develop a lasting flux, and draw blood from the groin, and anoint it with a caustic remedy.
And if it does not stop, cauterize with a wheel-shaped iron over the socket, having straight points. For a bruise.
Write the name of the owner on the hoof of the animal's affected foot,
and bind on a hemp cord, saying over each knot: 'I draw you into a bruise — be turned to stone, be turned to wood, be turned into a knot.'
And after tying the three knots, wind it around the animal's pastern, and again bind it with three plain knots, saying the same words, and then cut it with a knife and throw it on the ground.
Hippocrates's remedy for the same.

If a bruise occurs internally, these are the signs: if it lifts the front foot awkwardly and sets down the hoof hesitantly; or again, in the hind foot, if it walks gingerly on the tip of the hoof from both sides, and it is inflamed.

You will treat it thus: mark around the hoof, and if you perceive that it persists, apply as a poultice barley boiled in water, or knead hot bran and mix in a little old dung and apply that; and if it still persists, pare the hoof back.
And if the little bone in the frog of the hoof becomes visible, use honey and vinegar, and a little lint on a wick, for several days.
Then apply some astringent — cypress leaves ground with vinegar, or tamarisk leaves —

or likewise apply pomegranate rinds, boiled in vinegar and ground and applied; or chop them dry and sprinkle them on, or chop blue vitriol and oak-galls and sprinkle them on, having first washed the place with vinegar.
Pelagonius's remedy for the same.
Hang a small iron ring, engraved with a lion and a star above it, beneath the throat, and you will marvel at the result.
A soft remedy for sores.

Sixteen staters of wax, two staters of Colophonian resin, eight staters of fresh pig fat and eight of goat fat, two staters of boiled pitch, one drachm of litharge, three obols of split alum, four drachms of frankincense-manna, two obols of myrrh, half a cup of honey, two obols of male frankincense, three obols of galbanum, one cup of oil. Boil, adding the wax, the fats, the resin, the oil, and the pitch, then the honey.
When it is blended, then add the rest, finely ground, and boil it — [lacuna] — until, testing with a feather dipped in it, it sets on the fingernail.
And then take it off the fire and pour it into another vessel.
Its sediment is suitable for humans too, applied on lint to foul sores, and it also removes bruises, and is generally useful for the rest, except for fresh wounds and burns.
In veterinary use, when applied, it keeps flies from settling.
Another soft remedy.

One cup of oil, sixteen staters of wax, three staters of Colophonian resin. Boil these, pour into another vessel, and use it, dissolving the remedy in oil and applying it to the bare, chafed patches, and it will heal.
A poultice for proud flesh, good for excess growths, and for drawing up hollow sores.
Mix equal parts of lime, pine-resin, chalcitis, and vetch-meal, grind fine, and use; or use asphodel.
Pomegranate rinds, chopped and sifted, are also useful.
Cleansing remedies for sores.
Chop wild hemp and apply as a poultice, or asarum root, or bitter-vetch meal with good honey, or chop spurge with niter and honey, or use scorpion-tail plant with niter.
Mix barley meal with chopped cabbage leaves and apply as a poultice.
This most quickly clears away the scabby crusts from the back, or the so-called 'nails.'
Another.
Horehound with the so-called frankincense-herb, together with niter, does the same.
Chop cypress or germander leaves and apply.
Use equal parts of lime and chalcitis, or birthwort, or use wild hemp, dried and chopped.
For worms in sores.
Chop chamaeleon-thistle root and sprinkle it on, or use blue vitriol and lime in equal parts, for it does the same.
Another, for sores.

This too is excellent for burns and other sores: two drachms of blue vitriol, two and a half drachms of split alum, one drachm each of copper ore and chalcitis, half a drachm of verdigris; grind these fine and pour on white vinegar.
Boil it in a copper vessel until it boils up, and grind again, adding one drachm of myrtle, half a drachm of pomegranate rind, half a drachm of oak-gall.
Grind these, store them, and use with vinegar.
Another.

Soak pomegranate rinds for a day and a night in dry dark wine, so that the wine covers the rinds; boil, pouring in olive-lees twice the amount of the wine, and grind and strain it, discarding the woody bits, and, mixing alum and frankincense into the strained liquid, boil it.
Bring it to the thickness of honey, store it, and use it with vinegar.
And as the sore heals, make the remedy into a soft wax-salve.
A wax-salve.
An excellent plant for swellings, abscesses, sinuses, and wounds, especially those affecting the sinews, and for sores lacking skin or flesh.
It is called 'althaea,' by some 'molochē' (mallow), in Latin 'hibiscus,' and among the Sarmatians, Getae, and Thracians 'arispis.'
One must dig up the root, remove and discard the pith, and, roasting the rest, mix it with lard, pound it together, and, spreading it on a cloth, apply it.
It works the same way on humans too, and especially closes up sinuses.
Those who boil it are mistaken, for boiling takes away its potency; althaea is not easily found, growing everywhere in the regions of Asia or Sicily.
It is found at Smyrna, by the river Meles.
There is another plant called 'anadendromolochē' (tree-mallow), by some called 'salki,' whose leaf is broader.
Prepare its root in the same way as written above, and use it.
For it will provide the same effect in some cases.
A caustic remedy.

Two drachms of orpiment, one drachm of copper scale, two drachms of realgar; grind these fine, each separately, with cedar oil — if you have no cedar oil, grind with wild-cucumber juice instead, for it does the same. Another.
Two drachms of salt, rock-salt preferably, and one drachm of orpiment.
Another.
Two drachms of hellebore, an equal amount of roasted chalcitis; pour on honey and use.

One cup of honey, four cups of boiled olive-lees, one stater of burnt and finely ground sackcloth, an equal amount of birthwort, one stater of burnt papyrus; grind and put into a pan and boil until thoroughly cooked.
And when it sets, take it off promptly — otherwise it will scorch — and pour it into another vessel. Use it. A dissolving remedy.
One part dove dung, a quarter part niter, and twice the amount of the dove dung in prepared goat fat, and more fat —

grind the salt, the niter, and the dove dung together with sharp vinegar, and then chop and add the fat to it all, along with the wax-salve, and, grinding it all together, spread it on linen and apply it to strains of the sinew at the hip-joint, extending it to the swollen knot above.
It is excellent too for groin swellings in their early stage, for erysipelas, for dog-bites, and for the genitals when there is inflammation, spread on linen. A cleansing remedy for sores.
Chop cultivated raisins, vetch-meal, and wild-cucumber root, mix them, pour on honey, and use.
Let the cucumber be slightly more in proportion.
A fatty compound.
White lead and litharge, equal parts of each: put the litharge into a mortar and grind it first, then the white lead, and, grinding, pour on, adding alternately, oil and wine, enough for use.
Let the wine be white and fragrant, and the oil good.

It is good for all four-footed animals: applied on lint it draws up hollow sores and cleanses foul ones; and for draught animals as for humans it works well for chafing and abrasions, eruptions, weeping sores, flesh-deficient sores, bare patches, and hollow sores when used on lint, and for burns.
Another fatty compound.
One ounce of litharge, one ounce of white lead, one ounce of pig fat, enough rose oil.
Grind the litharge and the manna first, then the white lead.
Another: three ounces of pig fat, three ounces of white lead, three ounces of litharge, three ounces of wax.
Grind copper flower in boiled vinegar brought to the thickness of honey.
An excellent remedy for foul sores and spreading ulcers.
Boil portable alum with honey and use it on lint; use it the same way on humans too.
Boil it over a gentle fire, for it rises quickly.
For wounds and sores.
For wounds and sores that arise spontaneously or from some cause, and for splinters lodged in the feet at the sinew, it is an excellent remedy to anoint them with fine salt and liquid pitch.
For a snail-like growth on a draught animal, and for proud flesh.
[Lacuna] parts of verdigris, two of red ochre, one of chalcitis, one of blue vitriol; grind, sift, and sprinkle on. For sores.

Eleven ounces of rush oil, eleven ounces of wax, eleven ounces of goose fat, four ounces of hyssop, six ounces each of verdigris, galbanum, and orpiment, six ounces of resin, one ounce of storax, one ounce of Colophonian resin, one ounce of turpentine, one ounce of manna, one ounce of pine-cone, one ounce of red ochre, four ounces of fine wheat flour, enough wine.
Xenocrates's flesh-building remedy.
Ten ounces of iris, twenty ounces of vetch, five ounces of frankincense, five ounces of birthwort; grind them all separately and then mix.
A powder made with walnuts.
Grind equal parts of green walnut husk, lime, and wine-lees, and use.
Eumelus, for various sores.
You will treat sores of every kind by taking up ash of cyclamen root with barley meal and honey, and storing it for use.
But if they are deeper, mix red ochre with honey, anoint lint with it, insert it into the wounds, lay a cloth over it, and place a sponge soaked in vinegar-and-water on top, and bandage it.

Ground oak-galls also heal, and the juice of horehound with soot, or the peel of red apples, or vine-bark, burnt, reduced to ash and ground fine; roast one ounce of barley meal and add it, with six ounces of resin, four cyathi of wine, and an equal amount of oil; boil together and apply warm to the wound.
In this way varicose legs in humans are treated too.
But if inflammation follows, grind wild-cucumber root and wild fig-tree leaves with vinegar and honey, and apply.
And if the sore is found to be foul, grind spurge with honey, niter, raisins, and vetch-meal, and apply.
And if the bowels are ulcerated and discharge clean pus, you will treat it thus: three grams of sulphur, three grams of asphalt, cumin, and sagapenum gum,
grind and mix with wine, add it to the rest, and, dividing the remedy over nine days, insert it through the left nostril.
On sores in the mouth.

Sores in the mouth are treated with chopped red oak-gall, the tongue being held so that the remedy can settle in place; then wash it off with a sponge soaked in wine and rub it dry. On hairs growing in wounds, and on rabies in cattle.

If hairs growing in a wound prevent it from scarring over, grind a crab and wild raisins in vinegar, warm it, and apply to the wound; or grind Syrian sumac with orchid-root and ammoniac salt together, mix in honey, boil, and use.
The same is useful for cattle afflicted with rabies too.
Theomnestus, for putrefying sores in the mouth.
Grind chalcitis, roasted until red-hot, with honey until it becomes very fine, put it into a box, and use it for putrefying and spreading sores in the mouth and elsewhere.
For proud flesh, a modeling remedy: unwetted lime, chalcitis, vetch-meal, all equal, and pine-resin; having them fine, sprinkle on.
This also fills in hollow sores.
Easily obtained wound-remedies.

We have devised simple remedies, since it often happens on journeys that draught animals are wounded and one has no ready supply of costly compound medicines — useful to everyone, and easily obtained by people of modest means; for sometimes people cannot afford to treat with costly abundance, their poverty cutting them short.
For any significant bleeding wound, then, this is available: take up the so-called 'earth-guts' (earthworms) from unturned soil, and apply to the wound. Another.
Take round birthwort, well chopped and ground, grind it again together with honey, fill the wound with it, and bandage it. Another.

Put the inner bark of the elm into a pot of water and boil until well cooked, and, having ground it carefully in a mortar, insert it into the wound and bandage; but if it becomes inflamed, grind Cimolian earth with vinegar and smear it on the inflammation.
A styptic powder.
Often, when a draught animal is struck by a significant blow, the blood vessels are severed, from which hemorrhage results, and if this is not stopped, the animal will be in danger.

We have therefore devised an easily obtained powder that everyone can prepare: take rough sea-growths, soak them in liquid pitch, burn them, keep the ash, and fill the severed vessel with it, and bind it without pressing too tight.
For it works excellently. Another.
Orpiment, lime, chalcitis, and blue vitriol, four equal parts; grind fine and use.
A filling powder for sores.
Nothing prevents physicians from also caring that the scars of sores be neat.
For a scar, when it becomes hollow on a place that has suffered a cut, brings no small disfigurement.
It brings unbearable disfigurement, and ridicule upon those who treated it.

We shall therefore set out an easily obtained flesh-generating remedy for a hollow sore: make fine, clean flour from bitter-vetch, knead it with water, and bake little loaves until charred; mix in a third part of very fine, unburnt savory, and use.
Another.
Of the finest and smoothest frankincense, the so-called manna — [lacuna] — and let their proportion be this: one ounce of orpiment, six ounces of savory, three ounces of manna.
Hippocrates's preparation for wounds.
About one ounce of chalcitis, one ounce of split alum, one and a half ounces of sarcocolla gum, three ounces of grape-cluster sumac, three obols of olive-lees.
Boil until reduced by a third, then add one cup of honey and one cup of vinegar.
Boil these together until it thickens, and use it as the wound-remedy.
On wounds.
As soon as you anoint it, add lard and oil, and, melting these, smear it on; or smear on wrestlers'-oil scrapings and sprinkle on vetch-meal, and wash it for three days, and it will then be healed.
On blows and wounds.

When struck by many blows, ulcerations and swellings result. One must therefore bandage the places that can be bandaged with a sponge soaked in unmixed wine, and smear the places difficult to bandage with potter's clay kneaded with vinegar, or chop nightshade in vinegar and, pressing it out, smear it on, or smear on Cimolian earth with wine-lees vinegar, or chop hemlock leaves and smear them on. A fatty preparation.
Grind equal parts of white lead and litharge in the sun, mixing in vinegar and rose oil.
On swellings.
Take Attic honey and smear it on.
Chop lime and walnut husk together into one, cool it, and use.
Another.
Fleabane, or pine bark, or germander, or cypress-galls, or the leaves of wild mallow, or the leaves of wild hemp.
An excellent remedy.
Burn stag horn, grind it, and add oil; or grind pine resin and sumac together, and use likewise. A caustic remedy.
Two drachms of hellebore, an equal amount of chalcitis, three drachms of lime, one drachm of orpiment; grind all together and use.
For every kind of sore.
Grind six ounces of myrrh, two cyathi of honey, and enough wormwood.
Boil oil and wax.
Let it cool, and sprinkle on the wormwood.
Knead everything together, spread it on a cloth, and apply it for three days. This is suited both to pain and to inflammation, for it is quite reliable.
A fragrant wound-remedy.

Two ounces of litharge, one ounce of turpentine, two ounces of male-frankincense meal, two ounces of dry pomegranate rind, two ounces of Colophonian resin, two ounces of storax, one ounce of opopanax, one ounce of copper ore, six ounces of mistletoe-gum.
Preparation of a powder.
Five ounces each of split orpiment and lime, enough burnt pig bone.
Another, for savage mange.
Four ounces each of asphalt and unfired sulphur, four ounces of vinegar; boil until reduced to a quarter.
This also stops lichen.
Ounces of pig fat, wax, and sulphur, two ounces; grind what needs grinding and add it to the meltable ingredients, and, mixing it all, boil and anoint.
Another.
Six ounces of the barley that grows in stables, grind it with thistle, add enough henna oil, warm it, and rub it on while the sun is hot.
Another.
Boil frogs in water, take up their broth, add enough oil, boil together, and use.
Another, a highly effective remedy.
At the outset, apply seal fat.
But if it has already hardened, one must use more vigorous and stronger remedies.

For this use: dissolve and combine asphalt, sulphur, vinegar, liquid pitch, and old lard in equal weight, and apply — but only after first scraping off the mange with an iron tool and washing it with human urine.
Hippocrates, for madness.
It arises from bile, or from severe pain.
These are the signs: when led, it holds back; its movements become untimely, its ears prick up, and it lets its legs go slack.
The little veins along the nostrils turn red, it crashes into walls, wrenches away from whoever is leading it, and stands bolt upright.
It is treated thus: draw blood and drench with wine-and-oil — [lacuna] — give it at intervals of days, and drench with the same remedies.
Do not give it barley for ten days.

And if, from some cause or from soothing treatment, the underlying condition that produced it becomes more moist, give the drenches and bloodlettings according to the animal's age, reducing them for some, adding to them for others.
Eumelus's liniment for opisthotonos.
One ounce of bay-berries, one ounce of niter, four ounces of sheep-pitch, two ounces of wine, two ounces of oil.
A preliminary drink for the same.

Two ounces of bay-berries, one ounce of niter, three ounces of frankincense meal, one ounce of Gallic hartwort, two ounces of white pepper, two ounces of parsley, four ounces of opopanax root; chop and sift all these, dissolve in wine and oil, warm it, and give as a preliminary drink, and thus you will save the suffering animal. Treatment for tetanus.
One ounce each of wax, resin, and opopanax, one ounce of lard, one ounce of bay oil, three ounces of finely ground chaste-tree fruit; use.
A liniment for opisthotonos.

One ounce of wax, four ounces of resin, two ounces of opopanax, two ounces of stag marrow, three ounces of storax oil, four ounces of bay oil; boil all these together and use in the sun or some other warm place.
Horse. Another.
One ounce each of wax, opopanax, and oil; boil these together, and after boiling add enough vinegar, and use as described above.
Three ounces of bay-berries, cumin, and unfired sulphur, one ounce of resin, two ounces of common oil; mix all these and use. Another.

Before all else, let it stand in a warm place, and let these preliminary drinks be used: two grams of white pepper, one gram of saffron, one gram of myrrh; make all this into a lozenge. A liniment for the same, and for cold.
Wax, rose oil, and oil, some ounces, enough old wine.
A preliminary drink for the same.
Two ounces of liquid pitch, one ounce of bay-berries, half an ounce of matron's niter, one ounce of frankincense meal, one ounce of all-heal root, two ounces of wine, one ounce of oil.
Grind all these, mix with the wine and oil, and give.
Six ounces of bay-berries, one ounce of niter, one ounce each of frankincense, Gallic hartwort, and parsley; chop and sift all, and give with a warm drink.
Another, for ant-warts.
Three ounces of copper ore, one and a half ounces each of gum, chalcitis, and portable alum; mix in enough of the first-run soap-lye, and form into lozenges.
An eye powder.
Put brass plates and fresh urine together into a new earthenware dish.
Boil it, adding the urine until the plates dissolve, and use. Another.
Grind together ammoniac salt, cuttlefish bone, and crocodile dung into one, pound it fine, put it into a bronze vessel, and blow it into the eye.
An eye powder.
Grind fine niter and another fine substance together into one, and use for the eye.

If it develops sunken eyes from green fodder, treat it thus: draw blood from its forelegs and from the crown of the head, and use eye-plasters, and bathe it with crushed crab mixed with mallow leaves.
If you have no crab, use rainwater with goat's milk; if you have none of this, crush a root (obscured in the manuscript) with one ounce of wine.
Do this until it is healed.
Or treat it thus: foment with warm water twice a day, and mix goose fat with roses and anoint with it, and use it this way. An eye-remedy.
An eye treatment.
Grind six ounces of saffron, one ounce of myrrh, one ounce of pepper, with good honey, and put it into a bronze box.
For a white spot on the eye.
Burn a lizard, grind it, add enough honey, and use.
Another.

For an inflamed eye, frankincense-starch mixed with Attic honey should be applied; or add an equal amount of butter; or blow in ground cuttlefish bone through a reed; or anoint twice a day with silphium root in oil or pitch.
For every affliction of the eyes.
Roasted, ground salt, mixed with water and applied, is well suited.
Hippocrates's eye-remedy.

Grind soda-foam, African oil, onion juice, and honey together into one, and use; or burn white wine-lees, grind them fine, and smear on with honey; or burn copper ore, grind it fine, and use — but do not apply too much, lest it burn; apply it where there is no open sore. Or: one drachm of saffron, an equal amount of myrrh, half a drachm of pepper, an equal amount of reed-mace flower, three grains of pure frankincense, half a drachm of ammoniac salt; mix with honey, grind fine, and use for white spots, where there is no open sore.
Best also is this: burn crocodile teeth, grind them fine, and use; or likewise burn scorpions, grind them fine, and use.
For glaucoma and cataracts.
Burn greasy wool with barley, grind it fine, and use equal parts of each with roasted salt and honey.

One ounce of old lycium, an equal amount of Molossian wine, one spoonful of honey, one ounce of viper's-bugloss root, one ounce of germander, one ounce of ammoniac gum; grind fine, boil together, and use.
For flux of the eyes.
A green eye-plaster.
Mix old wine, egg white, and barley meal, and apply to the eye; or mix oil with the egg.
An eye-plaster.
One ounce of soft plaster, one ounce of myrrh from the Troglodyte country, one ounce of fine pollen, into egg white.
One ounce of iris, one ounce of manna, egg white.
Hierocles's preparation of eye-salves.
Burn an oyster-shell, pound and sift it, mix with honey, and use.
For attacks of flux in the eye, apply rose oil that has risen to the top, and egg white.
Another.
Mix sea-niter with old oil and use.
Another liquid remedy, marvelous for old and chronic white spots.
Six ounces of lycium, half an ounce of pure frankincense, two drachms of saffron, enough dry wine.
Add the dry wine and the ground and sifted frankincense and saffron; then grind the lycium, take it all up together, and use.
For ulceration of the eye.
Six grams of starch, two grams of violet, one and a half grams of gum; grind in water, take it up, and rub on with a whetstone dipped in water.
For ulcerations, severe pain, and attacks of flux.
Four drachms of washed white lead, eight drachms of starch, one and a half drachms of gum; grind and take up with spring or autumn rainwater, and use. Eye-salves for fistula.
Make equal parts of pimpernel juice, horehound juice, the ash of burnt cabbage, burnt dill root, and first-run soap-lye; grind them first, form into eye-salves, and use.
Another.
Grind iris, chamaeleon-thistle, birthwort, and gum in water, form into eye-salves, and use.
Another, that works well and removes calluses from deep down, drawing out fistulas along with the bone. Two ounces of roasted chalcitis, three ounces of burnt copper ore, one ounce of ammoniac gum.
Boil the ammoniac gum in sharp vinegar, and mix in the chalcitis and copper ore, already ground.
Then grind and form into eye-salves, some elongated and tapering, some round, and, storing them in a glass jar, use as needed.
Another.
Two ounces of verdigris, three ounces of orpiment, one ounce of gum.
Dissolve the gum in vinegar, grind the orpiment and verdigris beforehand, mix them in, and form into eye-salves, and use.
Another.
Two ounces of verdigris, half an ounce of burnt copper, chalcitis, dove dung; soak the gum in one cyathus of vinegar, then grind it all and form into eye-salves.

One and a half ounces of red niter, four ounces of roasted chalcitis, two ounces of wine-lees, six ounces of ammoniac gum, one and a half ounces more ammoniac gum; melt the ammoniac gum with the first-run soap-lye, then mix in the ground dry ingredients, form into shape, and use.
Another.
Form the juice of mistletoe-gum alone, and use.
Another.
Mix in first-quality honey and ground frankincense.
Another.
First-quality honey, or antimony, hemlock, and chalcitis, in equal parts; mix together.
Another, a good eye-remedy.
Three ounces of sweet wine, the whites of three eggs, three ounces of oil; mix all and use.
For scars in the eyes.
Grind one and a half ounces of spikenard, three ounces of ammoniac salt, twelve ounces of hyssop, half an ounce of cadmia, one ounce of pepper, and use.
For a tear of the eyebrow.
Pin together the edges of the tear, and store manna mixed with egg, and use it as a tested remedy.
For an attack in the eyes.
One obol of myrrh, one obol of crocodile dung, ammoniac salt, half an obol of cuttlefish bone, two cyathi of Attic honey; grind all these and use.
For hardened swellings of the eyelid.
Six grams each of myrrh and saffron, two grams of crocodile dung, enough Attic honey and stag marrow.
A boxwood eye-salve.

Two ounces of balsam, two ounces of saffron, two ounces of myrrh, four ounces of salt, four ounces of copper scale, two ounces of cuttlefish bone, one ounce of soda-foam, one ounce of sea-anemone, one ounce of Attic honey. A reddish eye-salve.
Two ounces of hyssop, half an ounce of saffron, two ounces each of white pepper, male frankincense, gum, and oil.
For ophthalmia in its early stage.
Four grams of rue, four grams each of male frankincense, dove dung, myrrh, oil, and first-quality honey, one gram of rose oil.
A poultice for the eye.
Mix bull-hide glue with half an ounce of asphalt, enough fine-wheat leaven, four ounces of frankincense meal, and enough vinegar.
For removing a white film.
Chew ivy leaves and spit onto the eye, for three days.
For scars in the eyes.
Rub with the saliva of a fasting person and salt, and they will thin out; or grind cuttlefish bone with salt and use; or press wild mustard seed through a linen cloth and drip the juice into the eye.
Every pain of the eyes is relieved by anointing with unsmoked honey.
And if unsmoked honey cannot be found, at least use honey smoked with incense.
And if none of these can be found, burn the surface of an old hide, make it into a powder, apply it to the eyes, and use it as a tested remedy.
An excellent eye-salve.
Three grams of myrrh, three grams of saffron, three grams of white pepper, two grams of black pepper, two grams of balsam, six ounces of Attic honey, three grams of celery.

The whole liver of a toad, a whole gerbil, six ounces of bay-berries, four ounces of myrrh from the Troglodyte country, three ounces of saffron-sediment, two ounces of cress seed, one ounce of red poppy-juice, two ounces of male frankincense, two ounces of quince-earth, two ounces of aloe, one ounce of dried roses, three ounces of larch-resin; grind these all together and use. Hippocrates, for pain of the heart.
While standing, heavy sweat breaks out over its whole body, and once it lies down on its side it rises again with difficulty.
It does not live more than a day.
For foot-gout.

Write these four names on a tin plate with a stylus that has not been polished smooth, and on a Sunday bind it to the foot that hurts; and again after thirty-six days — which falls, thirty-six days later, on a Sunday — undo it. [The words to be written are illegible in the source.]
Another.
Write two tin plates in the same way; throw the first one where it cannot be reached, and, sitting down there at once, bind on the other.
Do this eleven times.
And the last time, bind on nothing, having observed — both you and the one wearing the amulet — living things, one at a time.
For it is possible that the one wearing the amulet does not know letters.
But if he does know them, he binds it on for himself.
By the same author, for hemorrhage.
The juice of green coriander stops the flow of blood through the nostrils.
Hierocles's remedy for the same.
Coat a sponge with pitch, burn it, grind it with vinegar, and smear it on the navel.
Then apply white lead, and it will stop.

Pelagonius, how one must check an excess of blood from the animal's palate: and if unable to stop the blood, wash a small sponge in cold water and apply it to the head, the mouth, and the loins, and moreover foment the genitals with cold water too.
And if these cannot check the flow of blood, mix equal parts of black acacia gum and frankincense meal into very sharp vinegar, and apply it over the whole head.
For those bleeding from the nostrils.
Burn lentils and wool soaked in oil, and, grinding their ash, blow it into the nostrils through a reed.
An eye-remedy.

One ounce of orpiment, one ounce of myrrh, three ounces of white pepper, three ounces of long pepper, three ounces of saffron, six ounces of zinc oxide, three ounces of starch, three ounces of balsam-sap, three ounces of cuttlefish bone, enough honey.
A compound eye-plaster.
One ounce of saffron-sediment, one ounce of manna, three ounces of pollen, ten eggs, one ounce of African bulbs, enough vinegar.
An eye-remedy.

Two ounces of myrrh, two ounces of saffron, one ounce of spikenard, two ounces of cadmia, two ounces of zinc oxide, two ounces of white pepper, six ounces of Attic honey, six ounces of asparagus root, three cyathi of Falernian wine. Another: ten ounces of zinc oxide, three ounces of burnt lead, three ounces of opium, three ounces of Attic honey.
Bring all these listed ingredients into a mortar and grind them for the animal; then, mixing them, transfer them into a lead vessel and anoint the animal.

If it cannot be treated this way, draw a sufficient quantity of blood from its temples, and anoint it with the same remedy until it recovers. Four ounces each of washed zinc oxide, myrrh from the Troglodyte country, Sicilian saffron, and white pepper, three ounces of orpiment, two cyathi of water, two more ounces of orpiment.
Burn a lizard, grind it, add enough honey to it, and anoint with it this way. A compound: boil pig's trotters until they become tender, and, straining, give as a drench.
And if it still coughs, boil one ounce of goat fat and one ounce of vetch-gruel, and drench.
And if it still coughs, one ounce of sheep fat and one ounce of shellfish.
Use each of the above remedies for three days.
And if it still coughs, boil one ounce of pig fat and three ounces of must, and drench for three days, and the cough will stop.
Alexippus's Chironian remedy for every kind of cough.

I maintain that a swallowed remedy does no good, but that those who do such things are merely deceived — whether by bones or by whatever else — and even beguile their own eyes; but the windpipe and the throat become roughened.

One must therefore feather the throat, having brought the bull's-pizzle preparation through a mouth-gag; let it be soaked in honey and lowered down to the base of the windpipe, while above it a drench of equal parts vinegar and rose oil is given, so that it may be astringed and cooled.
And let it be boiled and applied again the next day.
Six ounces of liquid pitch, four ounces of unfired sulphur, six ounces of peeled garlic, six ounces of ground green leek, three ounces of lard.

Boil these together, strain, and add four ounces each of bay oil, henna oil, and iris oil; stir well and let it stand overnight, and shape three ounces of unsalted old lard into it, and soak it and anoint with the remedy.
Give it for three days, so that half of the remedy is worked in with the eye-salves.

I predict this: as the bull's-pizzle preparation passes into the throat as far as the windpipe, any blockage, wherever it has settled, will be dislodged by the pressure of the preparation and will come out below through the rectum, or the cough will expel it outward, if it is lodged fast. Another, given with lard, for chill and for attacks of venomous creatures, and for stirring up swellings, for six days, for one pair of draught animals.

Twelve ounces of lard, six ounces of fenugreek, six ounces of ground vetch, six ounces of lupine meal, four ounces of honey, one ounce of liquid pitch, six ounces of good wine; mixed together these suffice, and let it be shaped into pastilles and given for six days, and afterward let wine be blown over it.
The whole recovery, with this remedy given, lies in rest.
I have written these things from experience.
For cough: two ounces of butter, four ounces of liquid pitch; mix together and anoint with the bull's-pizzle preparation.
Another.
Soak eggs whole, shells and all, in very sharp vinegar, and give them whole, using plenty of vinegar, so that the eggshells dissolve.
For the stomach, for difficult breathing, and for cough.
One ounce of soapwort root, one ounce of elecampane root (that is, 'rhastos'), one ounce of anise seed, and, for each ounce of the above, sixty-one grains of pepper, and enough honey.
One must take two spoonfuls in the morning, one spoonful after the midday meal, and two spoonfuls in the evening.
Eumelus's remedy for a recent cough.
This heals a recent cough, and so on, restoring it to natural health.
It is a well-tested natural remedy if you bind one whole wild dock plant, with its leaves and roots, into a cloth and hang it around the neck.
Use this as a tested remedy.
For chronic cough.
Treat chronic cough by purging the belly, inserting fragments of wild cucumber, or two bean-sized balls of turpentine resin.
Mix half a squill with half a cup of water and insert through the nostril.
On ulceration of the windpipe from coughing.
If the windpipe is ulcerated deeply, it becomes rough, and the animal coughs very frequently and does not take food as it should.
For the part conveying it is ulcerated, and the animal neglects feeding and suffers for it.

The treatment for this affliction is as follows: it is drenched with a decoction of figs in water, reduced to a third, with two eggs mixed into the water, the water being no more than one Italian ounce, and using no fewer than thirteen figs.
Or the juice of vetch-gruel, well boiled, then, beating two or three eggs into the juice, drench through the mouth, one Italian measure.
Another remedy.
Mix horehound with myrrh, frankincense, old wine, and also first-quality honey, and drench. For a more severe cough in a horse.

And when you perceive that its mouth breathes badly, or that tears fall from it unaccountably: four ounces of manna, four ounces of myrrh, two ounces of frankincense, one ounce of saffron, one ounce of tragacanth, four ounces of skimmed honey, one bundle of hyssop; mix all with old wine and drench, and, until it recovers, give it warm water to drink.
For cough.
One must give the animals eggs that have been boiled, for three days, put into vinegar.
Give one of these each day.
For cough and heaviness of the head.
Rose oil, or a little first-quality oil, with warm water, through the nostrils, for several days. For bulb-like swellings, a similar remedy.
Grind and chop together saffron, Gallic garlic, linseed, fenugreek, and barley meal, and make into little balls; give with honey or liquid pitch.
A similar treatment.

Grind horehound (which the Romans call 'marrubia'), and mix it with a little oil and salt, and also sweet wine, and drench it this way. An excellent remedy for dry cough, or for a constricted windpipe, and for breathing and spasms.

Hyssop, fenugreek, tragacanth, Gallic garlic, half an ounce of green rue; boil all in water and reduce to a third, and give to the coughing animal for three days, and to one with pneumonia-cough for nine.
A similar remedy.
A saucer of dill, a saucer of iris, one gram of rue, a quarter measure of oil; mix and give through the mouth first thing in the morning.
Very useful for cough and for pneumonia-cough, that is, pneumonia.

Two ounces of all-heal root, one ounce of unfired sulphur, two ounces of male frankincense, four ounces of myrrh from the Troglodyte country, chopped together; from this preparation, pour two spoonfuls with two eggs and wine down the throat. For breathing, that is, for cough.

The plant that the Greeks call 'perdikion' and the Romans 'orkiolarem,' bay-berries, and five grams of wild-cucumber root, chopped and sifted together, drenched with half a pint of water and one cyathus of oil. Another, for a leech.
If it swallows a leech, lay it on its back and drench it with warm oil through a horn.
Once the liquid touches it, they will fall off.
And if it can be reached, whiten the hand with lime, and, taking hold of it with a sponge, cauterize it by heating iron and applying it.
Apsyrtus, on knowing whether a mare has conceived a male or a female.
Apsyrtus to Publius Paeanius, greetings.

I want you to know that among the Sarmatians it happens with some mares that, arriving at fourteen months from birth, the filly begins to have the movement of the natural purgation, and accepts the male, and conceives, and carries the foal for the same length of time as the others, and bears it alive, but suffers great pain in giving birth, so much that it cries out and groans.
And having given birth and seen the newborn, she flees from it and is afraid to approach it.

They therefore shut her into an enclosure and, having cleaned the foal, bring it to her, and then she is at last persuaded to suckle it and rear it to completion. It is also said to have been observed among them that, when the mare is close to foaling, if the udder slackens more on the right side (and the teat), she will bear a male, but if on the left, a female.
And when a mare being covered urinates on some plant, they mark and watch the spot, and if the next day they find the plant withered, they say that she has conceived.
And when it happens that a mare miscarries prematurely, they examine the mane. On the windpipe.
If the windpipe begins to trouble it, it breathes heavily and sends foam through the nostrils, and needs nothing but rest.
Give it, then, to drink for several days, until it recovers, five egg-shells, honey, one ounce of copper scale, one ounce of niter, and three ounces of wine.
Another remedy for pneumonia.
Boil a pig's trotter with water until it becomes like glue, and drench it through a horn.
Hippocrates, for the liver.
If anything happens to the liver, draw blood from its nostrils, from the—
These are the signs: it becomes entirely tremulous, draws up its flanks, falls down, and does not touch its food.
Abscesses will also form under the armpits, the eyes turn white, and it will develop diarrhea.
Such an animal will not live more than a day.
On a polyp in the nose.
If a polyp is troubling it, do nothing.
Spread bedding under it, so that it does not twist itself while rolling, nor become cast.

If it also begins to discharge blood from the nostrils, treat it thus: six ounces of frankincense, six ounces each of niter, opium, and rue, with one ounce of dry wine; drench it with this, until it is well.

Some say that one must bind three long needles together and, turning the head back, first pierce it repeatedly until everything comes out, then flush at once with wine and oil, and likewise on the following days, until it recovers.
On cattle.
If it ever happens that an ox becomes weak in strength, one should make crushed bitter-vetch and offer it.
Sprinkle it with water so that it is moist but not soaked, a half-choenix or a third of a choenix in quantity.
For whatever other ailments occur in them, let us use the remedies given for horses.
A drench for pneumonia-cough.
Seven grubs, two cyathi of oil, two eggs; mix all these into one, warm it, and drench.
Pelagonius, a simple and marvelous remedy for pneumonia-cough.

Into three ounces of spiced wine, having soaked half a pint of beans three days beforehand, and, grinding these thoroughly, administer through a horn for three days. For pneumonia-cough. Another remedy: soak beans in old wine, and after this, having ground it, add to it oil, half the amount of the wine, so that there will be three ounces of wine and one ounce of beans.
Grind all these together and give for three days.
Another.

Chop Gallic garlic thoroughly, and add the plant ironwort, which the Romans call 'parietaria,' and, grinding this thoroughly together with the garlic and old lard, make it into lozenges, and give these, unequal in number, for three days.
An excellent binding remedy for pneumonia-cough.

Two ounces of soaked tragacanth, half a pint of fenugreek, half an ounce of linseed — soak these three ingredients in water — and one ounce of goat fat, two ounces of stag marrow, half an ounce of dragon-arum root, one ounce of gentian, one ounce of centaury.

First, then, boil the soaked tragacanth and fenugreek, and also the linseed, in the same water they were soaked in; then, mixing and grinding all these together, put them in a pot with three ounces of must-syrup, and boil again. Another: boil a pig's trotter-tip in water with an equal amount of vinegar, and put this into a pot with three ounces of must-syrup and one ounce of already-soaked vetch-gruel, in such a way that the water in which the trotter-tip was boiled and the gruel soaked is boiled together with them; add to these bull-hide glue and four measures of sharp vinegar, and boil it all together until it turns into a broth.
Separately, boil the soaked tragacanth, fenugreek, and linseed in hot water, and, after boiling, grind them in a marble mortar, add the aforementioned ingredients, and boil these again.

After these have been thoroughly boiled, mix in the juice of parietaria, that is, ironwort, and stag marrow with goat fat, and, having boiled everything together as described, give it as a preliminary drink through a horn for seven or nine days.
Give this preliminary drink warmed, toward daybreak.
And if it is too thick, add a little more must-syrup.
For a recent case of pneumonia-cough.
Boil a ram's head in water until it entirely falls apart, and add a little honey to it, and from this give a drench through a horn to the fasting animal, for seven days.
For pain of the bowels.

One ounce of Gallic hartwort, four ounces of oil, one ounce of wine, two ounces of soft galbanum; six ounces each of opopanax, wax, Colophonian resin, turpentine, storax, bdellium, stag marrow, and propolis; six ounces of bull fat, one ounce of bay leaves, one ounce of manna, one ounce of old oil, six ounces of white pepper, six ounces of poppy, three ounces of ammoniac gum, one ounce of resin, one ounce of orpiment, one ounce of bay oil, one ounce of iris oil, one ounce of hyssop.
On internal spasm.

Horses or other draught animals that have some internal spasm develop hollow eyes and draw up their flanks, and, though they eat and drink, they grow thin, and when walking they take small steps, and while standing they bring their hind feet up close to their forefeet, and take longer to move.
If they urinate or defecate blood, or discharge their food through the nostrils, they are in danger.
One must treat them in the same way as the regimen for a consumptive animal. On enemas.
About two drinks' worth of cucumber juice, and a bean's-weight of an unnamed ingredient, dissolved in water and mixed with honey — give as an enema, and the effect will show. On enemas.
Mix wine-lees and honey, give as an enema, and walk it around, until the discharge stops.
On twisting of the bowels.
[The text here is obscure in the source:] let something take hold of the gut, cut off the heads and let it grow, then give centaury. On internal rupture.
It is worth going through more completely the cases of those that have ruptured something internally.
And that it is dangerous is clear, even if we do not say so.
If one of the limbs or the intestines is ruptured, this is the sign: it brings up dung through the nostrils, and sweats.
If it is the bladder, whatever it drinks it excretes immediately through the rectum.
If something happens to the lung, it brings up blood through the nostrils.
If something happens to the liver, the genitals swell, and the belly and the thighs.
If it is the spleen, it wastes away and does not take all its food.
If it is the kidneys, it urinates blood.
Now if one of the limbs is ruptured, or the bladder, you can do nothing to help.

But if the lung becomes affected, knead two choenixes of vetch-meal, adding a small saucer of salt, and shape it into bread; then burn it, grind it fine, and, when you give it to drink, sprinkle it into the drink.

Saffron, myrrh, Syrian nard, cinnamon, cassia, costus, slender birthwort, silphium-juice, celery, wild carrot, dog's-tooth grass, and elecampane; grind all these fine, pour on a saucer of honey and one cup of mellowed wine, and pour it in through the nostril.
Having drenched it three times at most, use the broth made from vetch-gruel.
You will settle the liver by giving pomegranate-juice and wheat flour to drink in winter, and barley flour in summer, and vetch-gruel.
For the spleen, make it walk, and give boiled figs.
For the kidneys, give the best fodder, and keep the animal at rest, and with the rest of the usual care.
How one must treat a horse that has developed worms in its intestines.
Such an affliction is recognized from the horse continually writhing about.
Prepare, then, this remedy: mix coriander juice with enough mustard, and a little opopanax, with honey-water and a little oil, and give it.
If a horse's bowels hurt, here is an unlikely-seeming but paradoxically effective remedy for this affliction.
If you write the horse's name with a stylus, it will be healed at once.
Preparation of an enema.

Bran-broth with niter, two grams of dried wild-mallow flower, half an ounce of oil and wine; and if it does not pass wind, you will add to the enema four grams of dove dung as well, and after the enema it will move about, and rest sufficiently afterward.
Before the enema, foment its belly with warm water.
A similar remedy: if it will not eat bird dung, slaughter a cock and give its belly, with the dung, raw, to the animal to swallow.
It is better still to dissolve it in wine and give it to the animal. Another.
If a horse's bowels hurt, spit into its face three times while fasting. A preliminary drink for those suffering internal complaints, tried by disease.

With this remedy, those with dry nostrils too are easily cured: give about two cyathi of roasted vetch-gruel juice for three days, and after this do as follows: take two ounces of hyssop, twenty dates, two bundles of green rue, six cyathi of fenugreek and beans; boil all in rainwater and give, having first warmed it. A preparation of wine.

Four measures of reed-mace flower, four measures of cassia-bark, four measures of myrrh from the Troglodyte country, liver-colored aloe, frankincense, pepper, and mastic; grind and sift each of these separately, then mix them well, and, taking two ounces of burnt gypsum, put it into two hundred ounces of wine, stirring; add three spoonfuls of the powder to the two hundred ounces, and stir gently for five days, and seal the jars, and shut up the doors and windows of the storeroom for six months, so that no draught enters.
Eumelus, on flux of the belly.
If the belly is loose, let blood be drawn from the veins in the head.
Let it drink warm water with barley meal.
Chopped pomegranate rind, given through the mouth, also checks a loose belly.
On purging of the belly.

If it is purged in the belly — this happens from too much running, from flatulence, or from bad fodder — treat it thus: bleed the veins in the head and those in the forelegs, until they run freely; or give water with barley meal, but not much barley; and lead it out for a walk, and wash it with not too much water.
If there is no improvement, resort to a drench through the nostrils, and, applying a poultice, having brought it to a boil, grind it with wine and drench continually after four days.
On ileus.
Those with ileus must be given an enema of a decoction of beets and niter-pebbles ground together with bdellium, and must be washed and covered with blankets, and a fire kept burning nearby.
Give as food, above all, green fodder or the softest hay.
And if this does not resolve the blockage, one must insert a smoothed hand and remove the obstructions.
Drench also with beet seed together with six cups of wine and oil.
And if the seed is not available, scrape the hooves of the forefeet, grind the scrapings with three cups of wine, and give it; and drench the nostrils too.
Having removed the obstructions, mix ground salt with honey and insert it into the rectum, as much as possible.

Concerning wild beasts: all the others are born, like humans, in the wombs of their females, but with elephants it happens only in the females; and female elephants carry in the womb for thirty months, but produce males in nine months; and all the other beasts are born within twelve months.
Pelagonius, on the number of teeth.

The horse has forty-two teeth [lacuna]; the sheep has twenty-one teeth; the billy-goat, that is the she-goat, has twenty-seven teeth; the bull has [lacuna] teeth; a man has thirty-two teeth, a eunuch has twenty-nine, a woman thirty.
Apsyrtus, on how long a mare is pregnant.
A mare gives birth, from conception, in [lacuna] months, ten days over.

And if it ever happens that she foals early, at nine months and twenty days, such a foal is still reared and brought to maturity; but they separate it from the herd, even if it is a female — for such early-born foals turn out undersized.
Give fresh lovage leaves, ground, to drink; but let it first abstain from food.
Give one ounce of bitter lupine with half an ounce of vinegar and half an ounce of myrrh-oil to drink, for nine days.
Hippocrates, on miscarriage of the embryo.
If it miscarries the embryo, it rolls about, and the belly becomes distended with wind.
Drench it with cumin and oil mixed together, a sufficient amount of each.
Drench the mare with fennel together with must-syrup and oil; likewise cut off the tips of the ears and drench, and set her right with cauteries.
On lameness at the knees.
If it becomes lame for no apparent reason, crush leeks in a mortar, boil them in water, and give this to drink mixed with niter, or purge it with cucumber root.

But if it originates from the head, cut a deep transverse incision down to the bone, four finger-widths from the hip-joint, and then insert a finger into the incision and move it along the leg, and if the finger strikes any sinew, divide it with a small knife, and dress the incision with liquid pitch and salt.
For pain of the head.
If there is pain of the head, it will show these signs: inflammation about the eyes, and it discharges through the mouth something like dough.
One must therefore foment its head with hot water, and let it have gentle rest.
Also draw blood from the eyebrows, and crush trefoil leaves and give them to it to drink.
If its eyes are staring, you will need to draw off blood from its neck, three ounces, then take some salt, stir it with water, and drench it.
If you do not have this, use earthworms: send two ounces of old urine, grind them into it, and drench through the left nostril.
Another remedy.
Apply barley meal mixed with resin.

You must also take care that the rest of the body be treated in rotation with other preliminary drinks, thus: chop up seven river-crabs, strain thoroughly with one ounce of goat's milk and one cyathus of oil, and give as a preliminary drink through the mouth.
And if you cannot find milk and river-crabs, make honey-water from three cyathi of honey and a weight of one obol of white pepper, two grams of saffron,
grind these together and give through the mouth.
Another remedy.
Give barley meal with a lozenge as we described, in summer; but if it is winter, give it the same way with wheat flour.
A horse: one must recognize from this that it has been struck in the brain, when it immediately suffers spasms and slavers, and thereafter shuns its food and strains its whole body forward.
One must bleed it at the temples, and apply African sponges with equal parts of vinegar and rose oil to its head.

Provide it with green fodder, and if it turns away from this, offer it ground beans with wheat flour, and pour honey-water down its throat through a horn, until it takes to the green fodder again, on which sprinkle a little brine.
Eumelus, for chafed feet.
If an animal suffers this, and so on.
This helps cattle too, and is fitting to apply to them.
It helps cattle to have their horns firmly coated with pitch.
For the animals' feet, give bitter-vetch with barley for many days; or chop and grind two parts of ivy seed to one part of round alum, and use.
Hierocles, on heat-inflammation of the feet.
Heat-inflammation occurs especially on frozen ground, causing the feet to hurt.

It is fitting to lance the foot that hurts, and, having fomented it, to apply as a poultice barley meal mixed in equal parts with wine, or to apply bran boiled in vinegar as a poultice, until it heals.
On tenderness of the hoof.

If a horse is tender-footed, wash and wrap linen on its hooves, and if this does not seem to strengthen them, melt lard and wax together, adding asphalt on top, and do this as often as it feels pain in its feet.
Or otherwise — which seems to me the better way — take, and so on.
For those wanting to cough but unable to, on account of a deposit of phlegm.
It easily happens that a horse is troubled by a deposit of phlegm, and the throat becomes blocked, and it chokes at the windpipe, and, wanting to cough, cannot.
The phlegm passes through the mouth, mucous and foamy.

It is helped by being drenched through the nostril with water-and-oil, or with niter in water, or with a decoction of figs in water, and let it be walked about until it shakes itself and tosses its head, so as to dislodge the phlegm, and then it is no longer in danger.
Hierocles's summer remedy for those coughing.
Frankincense, chopped and sifted, is given with wine, or in due proportion to the frankincense, one spoonful.
For a horse: six ounces of wax, two ounces of storax, five ounces of turpentine, ten ounces of bay leaves, one ounce of opopanax, one ounce of stag marrow, enough iris oil to bind it together.
Another.
Three ounces of opopanax, three ounces of storax, two ounces of rue, two ounces of saffron-sediment; drench with these.
If a horse also suffers distaste for its food, soak savin in water and wipe out its mouth with it.
Add mastic-tree leaves too, for their pleasant scent.
For runaway, rebellious horses.
Boil box-tree leaves, cedar, and hemlock in water, and, straining it well, give it as a preliminary drink, so that it falls asleep and forgets its own unruly temperament.
And after this wake it up and make it walk about.
And if it is also a kicker, use the same remedy, also applying cold water over the navel.
Use it as a most reliable remedy. Hierocles, on one bitten by a viper.
A dreadful viper's bite, smeared with spurge, is stopped.
O Chiron, how did this escape you? Not without skill did Quintus discover these four: gentian, bay-berries, myrrh, and birthwort.
If a mouse bites a draught animal, its whole body swells.
And if a shrew-mouse bites, it is worse if the shrew is unusually long or pregnant when it bites.
The bite itself festers into an ulcer.
Treat it thus:
grind large garlic cloves with niter.
If you have none, grind it with salt and cumin instead.
If the swelling grows worse, use vinegar and salted barley as a further treatment.
And if the sores become larger, soak the sores themselves, if you wish.
If these do not heal it, use the cautery.
For the bite of a reptile.
Burn stag horn, then grind it to about a cup; six ounces of bat-plant, six ounces of 'eklekebra,' six ounces of germander, six ounces of stag marrow.
Grind all these together into one in a mortar, then shape it into a cloth or a hide wrapping. For herpes.
If herpes occurs, two drachms of orpiment, one drachm of lime-lye; grind with vinegar and smear on.
Or half a drachm of chalcitis, an equal amount of blue vitriol, and a quarter of lime-lye; chop these and use with vinegar.
On mysiasis.
If you wish to treat it, take dried human dung, grind it, and sprinkle it on.
Another, from Severus.
The same, by Amasis, for making the hair on a scar match the rest of the body.
Take the plant called 'antikrokon,' which grows where water cascades down, similar to madder, and moss dried from a marsh; chop and sift them.
Then knead with butter, comb it through the hairs one at a time, and smear on — whatever the color of the animal; if it is black, use goat horn instead. Apsyrtus, on lice-infestation.
If lice occur in the mane or over the whole body, grind fresh hemlock foliage and rub it on.
Or chop cyclamen root, mix with oil, rub it on, and after one day wash it off with urine or a decoction of lupines, and, having washed it off, anoint the lice-infested parts with pitch-oil.
For cattle: if lice-infestation is in the mouth, it will be recognized thus: it cannot eat, and its tongue is extremely rough.
It is treated thus: chop fresh wild-cucumber root together with dried figs, and, wrapping it around the root, give it to eat, until it is healed.
Grind chamaeleon-thistle with wild raisins.
Grind it in the same mixture with the cucumber, put it into the mouth, and hold it shut, keeping it there for a while.

And if the affliction does not stop with these, one must lay the ox down, take hold of its tongue, and with scissors cut away the so-called 'lice' around it, which are rough growths resembling wild thyme.
Having cut these away, cauterize lightly with a flat iron, not too hard.
Eumelus, for tapeworms and other worms.
The kind of worms and tapeworms is accustomed to breed internally.
This is recognized by the animal's continual rolling about; it often turns its head toward its belly, and twists its tail.
And it is recognized by these signs.

One must therefore insert the hand into the belly, as we have said, and draw out the excrement together with the tapeworms, and put ground radish with one ounce of vinegar down the throat, and thus suffocate the worms and tapeworms.
For those occurring in either sex, male and female, and for those arising from wounds.
Sprinkle sharp brine on the barley about to be eaten by the animal.
Others boil radish in water and foment the genitals with the decoction.
They are also driven off by sprinkling cold water, or by adding horehound or leek juice. Wounds are treated with pitch, oil, and lard, and so on.
For tapeworms.

Roast as much coriander seed as the hand can hold, and, grinding it with warm water, pour it down the throat through a horn for three days; or cardamom seed ground with water and poured into the horse's throat does the same.
For sinews swollen from travel.
If they are recent, use fresh sponges with vinegar and Cyrenaic silphium-sap.
Apsyrtus, for the overworked and the emaciated.
One must help the exhausted and emaciated animal thus: crush about a choenix of white bitter-vetch, and soak the crushed vetch in four cups of fragrant white wine, and let it stand for one day.
From this, give a third of a choenix each day before watering the horse, for thirty days, and offer roasted barley, and its body will grow steady.
Let the measure of crushed vetch be well soaked.
By the same author, for those fighting each other at the manger.
When they become vicious toward each other at the manger and fight, so as to bite one another, the bites are soaked with fish-sauce, or brine, or vinegar-brine.
Bites that occur at the sinew easily cause lameness.
It is treated with marshmallow, as written above.
By the same author, for pain of the sinews.
If the sinews are in pain, use hot water and a plaster.
One must also soften it with gentle walking, soft rest, and cold applications.
Give the usual food.
Anatolius, on sinews.
Foment the sinews and the head of the afflicted animal with hot water.
Then, putting beef fat, myrrh, and sulphur into a small pot, cover its head and fumigate it, and warm it; and also purge the belly. Draw blood from the tail.
Apsyrtus's remedy for the same, in force.
Wash the tails of both animals and give both of them the water itself to drink, or dissolve the dung of each in water and give it to each other to drink.
Another, useful for thinness.
Gather couch-grass, the kind farmers often cut away with the plow, as much as you like, and, washing it thoroughly, give it daily with barley and fine chaff; it is useful.
For this is beneficial to foals still young in age too.
Chariton's warming liniment against fatigue works for kidney complaints, sciatica, paralysis, and all those suffering anything from chilling.
It also brings on menstruation when rubbed on the lower belly and hips.
It also treats colic sufferers when a folded compress is applied to the navel.

Two ounces each of castoreum, pepper, sponge-stone, spurge, pellitory, bay-berries, white mustard, galbanum, and opopanax; two ounces each of old oil; one ounce of Tarsian smoke-oil; three ounces of grape-must oil; three ounces of iris oil; one ounce each of bay oil and turpentine; two ounces each of wax and roasted resin; niter.
Melt the opopanax and the lard, strain them, and then mix.
Weigh out and add the wax, the resin, the lard, the grape-must oil, the iris oil, the bay oil, and the oil, and, having melted them, add the galbanum, well chopped.
And when the galbanum has also melted, add the turpentine, and melt it gently, and, straining, add it to the opopanax, then the dry ingredients.
When using it, mix in grape-must oil or iris oil with the remedy.
For colic and for menstrual complaints, use the remedy by itself.
Parthenius's remedy, which Domitilla affirmed she used continually.
It hardens the hooves, making them firm and free from injury.
The remedy suits young colts, whether unweaned, first-shedding, or second-shedding, so long as the hoof is still soft and receptive to the remedy.

Three ounces of burnt copper, two ounces of orpiment, three ounces of copper ore, two and a half ounces of unfired sulphur, four ounces of asphalt, three ounces of split alum, half an ounce of cedar-resin, one ounce each of squill and Colophonian resin, six or seven chopped mountain lizards raised in waterless places, two ounces of old lard.
