Pound and sift the dry ingredients, melt the meltable ones, and put in the lizards, chopped live in a mortar, and boil in a pot, and melt it all together.
Then stir it often with a spatula, so that it does not boil over, and do this out in the open.
For it has often boiled over and set the roof on fire.
As for the cedar-resin, once the mixed ingredients are moderately boiled, add it then and boil together, until it reaches the thickness of an ointment.
Then one must apply the remedy to the hooves, first rubbing and softening them, so that the remedy may penetrate close to them.
Do this for forty days.
The effect of the remedy becomes perceptible after ten days from when it is first applied.
For the hoof begins to change, starting from the coronet.
Having rubbed it in, one must not disturb the animals, but around the ninth hour, after watering them, rub it in and stable them, so that the remedy may work throughout the whole night.
After five days, exercise the animal.
When you apply the remedy, take care that it does not touch the hair of the coronet, for it damages the flesh.
One should also attend to the frogs of the hooves and pare them lightly with iron.
For from standing in one place, problems arise. On the joints.
If the joints are in pain, it will show these signs: it cannot walk or doze off, and it becomes inflamed from the joints themselves.
One must therefore use many remedies: smear on cress and wine ground to the size of a finger, and draw its blood; and, if that fails, lance it open.
That one must purge along with putting out to green fodder.
It is better to put a horse out to green fodder with cucumber and niter, and it will become stronger and better-conditioned from the pasture. On cattle.
The afflictions that occur in cattle, and the remedies for them, have been written most excellently by Mago the Carthaginian, in the Phoenician language.
It has also been written by others, whose accounts we shall set alongside, showing the most troublesome afflictions and their treatments.
Various afflictions trouble cattle. Eumelus, treatment of cattle, and on their preservation.
Caper, together with wild olive or myrtle leaves, and also cypress-gall, boiled in wine and given, provides equal preservation for cattle.
But first put the ingredients into water and leave them out under the open sky for one night to steep. On those troubled by the gadfly.
For an ox troubled by the gadfly, grind wormwood in water, and anoint the ox with it for several days, and it will keep off the gadfly; or grind it again and anoint.
Compounding of a plaster made with herbs.
Galbanum, and so on.
until it becomes a soft plaster.
Use it this way on the animal.
Use it.

For an abscess, once it has fully formed, with enough wine and oil, make this remedy warmer for winter use, and use it this way: when you anoint the animal, put straw beneath it around its body, and wrap a blanket over it, so that the plaster draws in its blood, so that it adheres firmly to the body itself.

If it develops a growth like verdigris, let it stand in a warm place, and give it warm water to drink and as much fodder to eat as the animal can take, until it shakes off the affliction itself, and anoint the animal daily, until it recovers. Hierocles's caustic remedy for slackening of the joints and for swellings in any place whatsoever, whether from a blow or some other cause or spontaneous, or for dissolving whatever hardnesses you wish, or dispersing recent sebaceous cysts.
Eight staters of asphalt, four staters of Colophonian resin, six staters of wax, one stater each of galbanum, opopanax, and lime; boil these together and, warming it, anoint.
Another gentle, relaxing ointment.
Six ounces of Colophonian resin, one ounce of lard, three asses'-weight of linseed, two asses'-weight of fenugreek, one measure of barley meal, half a pint of oil.
Knead a part of fresh lime and an equal part of burnt wine-lees with mastic-tree lye, or with fresh olive-stone ash from beans, or grind fresh iris and apply.

Three ounces of galbanum, three ounces of wax, four ounces of bdellium, five ounces of roasted resin, four ounces of oak mistletoe-gum, four ounces of ammoniac gum, five ounces of digestive Bruttian pitch, four ounces of stag marrow, three ounces of opopanax.

Florus's remedy: five ounces of Judean asphalt, five ounces of Attic propolis, six ounces of Babylonian bdellium, four ounces of oak mistletoe-gum, six ounces of Bruttian pitch, two ounces of henna oil, six ounces of galbanum, two ounces of frankincense-manna, three ounces of stag marrow, two ounces of pure wax, six ounces of ammoniac gum.
Another, for the hip.
Two ounces each of galbanum, opopanax, stag marrow, turpentine, bdellium, frankincense-manna, wax, bull fat, wormwood, Bruttian pitch, Judean asphalt, and digestive resin; mix and boil all, and use.
A caustic remedy for everything.
Two ounces each of galbanum, storax, Bruttian pitch, poppy, frankincense meal, bay-berries, Judean asphalt, turpentine, and Macedonian parsley.
For ozaena in draught animals.
Take the sweepings with which the oven is wiped and washed off into the vessel where the water is, gather it, and apply it in the sun, having first washed and cleaned the place with vinegar.
Hippocrates, on fistula.
When it becomes fistulous, one must remove it thus: if the place admits a small knife, that is best of all.

But if not, constrict its opening, grind burnt blue vitriol with very sharp vinegar to make eye-salve-like sticks, and, having dried them, insert an equal amount of mistletoe-gum with the salve-stick, and, grinding it, use.
Another.
Take the root of bear's-breech, scrape it, and spread it on; or grind wild-cucumber fine, or knead it with spurge-sap, and insert it. Another, for malignant sores.
One treats a malignant sore, if the affected part has not yet been treated with sap.
First one must cut around it with a small knife as far as possible. Hierocles, on fistula.

If it is in the shoulder-joints, and one of the joints settles against the cartilage — but if it settles anywhere else, whatever the place, cut it open and cauterize it, and treat it with the remedy made from lime, until the scab falls off.

Once the diseased tissue has fallen away, it gradually fills in again to its normal state; but if the fistula is on a tendon, use straight cauteries applied forcefully to the tendon, until the scabs fall off.
Treat it with a caustic remedy until the putrefied tissue falls away, and then let the sore fill in.
Pelagonius, if a horse develops a fistula at the coronet.
Mix copper flower with very sharp vinegar, and when it dries, insert it into the fistula.
Apsyrtus, against the evil eye.
'Go, I abjure you — depart, stand away from the horse whom his own dam bore, O bewitchment, as far as earth is from heaven!' For the affliction called 'wolf' in animals.
So that the first person to see it there should say: 'You have not escaped notice — you are a wolf.'
And this too: 'let it bite this place a third time, and let it bite once for all.'
Hippocrates, on bared bones — the remedy called 'the boiled one.'
Put four ounces of scraped verdigris, half a cup of honey, and one cyathus of vinegar into a bronze vessel, and boil until it becomes ointment-like.
This is called 'the boiled one.'
On a mule going lame from the kidneys.
When a mule goes lame in both hind legs, it has pain in the kidneys.

One must therefore cauterize it, and let the burn be in this place; then, with salt and ground star-anise-stone, and about a stater of Egyptian niter, dissolving these in about half a pint, treat it, mixing in a little Attic honey and oil.
For twisted sinews, boils, and for many other things.

A remedy for twisted sinews, boils, and painfully swollen glands, and for every kind of hardness: one ounce of old oil, one ounce of white salt, one ounce of white lead, three ounces of ammoniac gum, eight ounces of dry resin, three ounces of wax, six ounces of opopanax.
Pelagonius, on the loins, kidneys, and hips.
It is fitting for us to set down for your worthiness a few remarks on the loins and kidneys.
For this readily befalls an animal worked continually in this way.
For shared experience of suffering often discovers cures and passes them on.

We have very often seen you yourself, unclothed, with weakened kidneys, and so it is clear that you receive a double benefit from this same care and treatment; so that your own loins too may be strengthened by this chosen remedy — and a horse that is worn down by these same afflictions deserves the same care and treatment.
For the most part horses injure their loins through heavy loads, or when they leap over a ditch and it happens that their hind feet come down awkwardly.
This affliction also occurs in them from severe cold.
Then, therefore, one must treat them with these remedies: let the loins be fomented with warm water, and after this use a caustic remedy.
If it continues to hurt for a long time.
Open the veins of the hooves, and mix salt, lard, and oil with the blood that flows out, and apply it over the kidneys.
And if necessity demands it, use a soft plaster too, for nine days, and observe the progress of the treatment.
And if necessity calls for it, bleed from the groin, and then treat the hip with the remedy.
The remedy is this: four ounces of spurge, four grams of liquid pitch, four ounces of common salt; mix together and boil.
Another.
Take up water-mint with one ounce of barley meal in water, and store it.
An ointment for the chariot-harness gall, called 'koudrigarion.'
Two ounces each of all-heal sap, castoreum, and galbanum; one ounce each of turpentine, roasted resin, pine-resin, butter, Bruttian pitch, lard, henna oil, bay oil, and white wax.
For draught animals, equal to equal.
Grind mustard and dried figs in equal parts, and add enough vinegar to bind it, and, having pared the hooves white, apply as a poultice.
The same has also been made for, and treats, hard-footedness.
A drawing, hardening, and dispersing remedy.

Four ounces each of wax, mustard, bay-berries, and niter; eight ounces each of henna oil, turpentine, and oil. Chop and sift the niter, the bay-berries, and the mustard; melt the wax, the resin, and the oil, and sprinkle in the dry ingredients, warming it last. Another, for the feet.
Pound equal parts of roasted resin, asphalt, unfired sulphur, and hog's fennel, then mix them with chopped lard, adding vinegar.
Anoint it warm.
Apsyrtus of Clazomenae, horse-doctor, to his fellow-physician Moschion of Ciōs.
[Lacuna.] For horses' feet.
For horses' feet, boil wild-olive leaves and cypress leaves together, and mix.
And when it has boiled to a moderate consistency, mix in alum and use it as the treatment.
It usually causes the first hoof-growth to shed.
A compound for the feet.
Bramble root, or again worn niter, or spurge, or ironwort, or peony-seed, or black hellebore root, or onion, and, dissolving these and straining through linen, they drip them into the nostrils.
The quantity poured in is determined proportionally for each of the listed plants.
For the fresh ones are used as they are, but drench with the roots and the seed in prepared form.
A useful remedy for the feet.

Boil a live lizard in oil, and set it in wax; use it by smearing on with bull fat and pitch, and binding it in a pine-torch wrapping; or heat a potsherd and smear on. For discharge and clearing of the nostrils.
Crush radish and another ingredient.
If you wish to clear its nostrils after a chill, take three cyathi of fish-sauce and one cyathus of oil, and put two cyathi into the nostrils, and let it walk about.
Then put it in a hobble and tie it up, and let the discharge run down from its nostrils.
Eumelus, for a bone: grind cress seed with wine and good oil, warm it, and pour it in through the nostrils. Apsyrtus's gift: good, salutary, marvelous, and effective for draught animals too.

'Iao, Iae, in the name of the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit' — [voces magicae:] iriterliestather, nochthai brasax, salōlam nakarzeō maza areous daroucharaēl ablanathal bathiaketh dryth toumalath poumadoin chthou chthou, litiotan mazabatēs maner opsachiou ablanathaleba — 'Iao, Iae, in the name of the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.' Say this, and write it with a bronze stylus on a clean tin plate cut from a seal-tablet, and, binding it in tanned leather, fasten it wherever you wish.
Having written the plate, fumigate it with storax.

And make a drench of this kind: burn a live snake in a new pot with its mouth sealed shut, so that the potency does not escape; make ash from it. Burn also the 'kriptic' storax, and, having made an ash of it, mix it with dog's blood, ivory filings, pepper, and malabathrum leaf, with honey and fragrant old wine; drench with this, and you will find it of the greatest benefit.
Eumelus, for preserving the health of animals.
[An obscure clause in the source.] A preliminary drink given each quarter of the year — in spring, summer, autumn, and winter — preserves the health of all animals, horses especially.
The preparation is this: heliotrope leaves ground with half a pint of wine, one egg, and as much oil as two eggshells hold.
Warm these, then, and pour them in through the nostril.
It is extremely useful.
Or give three ounces of pig dung with one ounce of old wine.
From the remedies of Aspidius: a fatty ointment for sores on draught animals' necks.

From the 'juice' compound: six ounces of pig fat, six ounces of wax, ten ounces of soap, two ounces of oil; once the meltable ingredients have boiled together, sprinkle in litharge, put it into a shell-dish, and grind until it thickens, sprinkling as you grind; then put it into a mortar again and grind.
It will use up a quarter-ounce of Italian wine.
Then sprinkle on vinegar again, about half the mixture.
Then grind lead-ore, sprinkle it in, and grind until it comes together.
Use it.
This works for pigs and for all draught animals too.
On a mare.
If a mare miscarries: half a pint of vinegar, four ounces of Alexandrian vetch-gruel.
Roast the vetch-gruel and sift it very fine, and give it this way.
Apsyrtus, for lethargy.
When this disease itself begins, the animal collapses.
When it can no longer hold itself up at all, and especially when it begins, as it were, to snore, these are the signs of it: it sleeps excessively, its lower lip hangs loose, and it yawns.
The treatment, then, is to be rubbed by hand and to have wine and oil blown into it, and it will cease on the seventh day.
On epiploos.

This will be the sign of epiploos: it produces phlegm all over, and its eyes blink frequently. Draw blood from the neck and from the shoulders, and with that same blood mix salt, niter, and vinegar, and smear it all over in the sun for two days, and after this, on the third day, wash it with cold water.
And continue this treatment on it until it is free of pain.
On a horse panting for breath.
If it pants for a long time, this will be its sign: it will discharge from its nostrils, and its eyes will grow weaker.

You will treat it thus: draw off about a cup of blood from its neck, and foment it with hot water; use poultices of raw barley-meal spread on a cloth, and apply it this way, and give it as a drink vetch-gruel with calamint and pennyroyal, six ounces being enough; boil these together and give the needed amount through a horn.
Hierocles, on asthma.
If it is troubled by asthma, it evidently pants, and its flanks are drawn up and swollen, and the affliction is harmful and severe.
Boil a mina's weight of figs in water, and, having made three cups of the liquid, pour it in with two eggs through the mouth.
Do this repeatedly, until it recovers.
Apsyrtus, on gelding a draught animal.
If you wish to geld a draught animal, in the month of May, while the north wind is blowing, dig a pit, and bind its testicles, so that it does not become excited.
Then take a sharp iron blade and quickly cut open its skin.
Then, once its testicles come out, take care not to remove their roots.
Then bring salt and pound it, and fill the wound with it, and raise it up; and if you release it, see that it does not swell up.
The next day, treat it again in the same way.

If you see that it is not discharging, release it, and, taking pitch and oil, anoint it well over its kidneys, and likewise its head and nostrils, and do not let it walk about much, until it recovers.
And let it stand in a warm place, and anoint the whole body with frankincense-manna and wine, so that it does not collapse from the pain, and wrap a blanket around it.

If it discharges blood: ammoniac gum, an ounce, two cyathi of leek juice — this works very well, if you also mix in honey and silphium-sap. If it develops distressing tapeworms, treat it thus: crush one ounce of wormwood with salt and barley meal into a single broth and give it, and, meanwhile, wash out its mouth with water by hand, and give it good fodder, and give it drink too.
On the loins.
If the loins become chilled, one must pour much cold water over them from a height.
Do this too: one ounce each of heath seed, rue, and all-heal; mix with warm wine and give it to drink.
If it suffers throughout its whole body, it will at once become sluggish, and its member will droop, and its eyes will stare fixedly, and its hindquarters will seem bound up.
One must, then, with plenty of warm water, anoint it with oil and vinegar, and let it walk a little, and use frequent rubbings, and foment its forelegs with hot water.
If it begins to improve, give it as much food as it wants, and 'trisélinon' to drink.
The 'juice' compound.

Two ounces each of old pig fat, turpentine, and wax, four ounces of resin; two ounces each of pine-resin, old oil, and henbane juice, and marshmallow juice; boil for a long time until it no longer stains.
Add four ounces of varnish-resin, four ounces of galbanum.
Take it off the fire and stir it with a spatula for a long time.
The 'juice' compound.
Seven ounces of oil, six ounces of litharge, four measures of juices; boil until it changes color. The great 'barbara.'

Two ounces each of Judean asphalt, Bruttian pitch, wax, roasted resin, and common oil; three ounces each of litharge, white lead, and split and round alum; two ounces each of copper ore, oak-galls, and chalcitis; one ounce each of opium, opopanax, liver-colored aloe, myrrh, and frankincense; three ounces of mandrake juice, enough very sharp vinegar. Put the meltable ingredients into the mortar, and take them up, adding the dry ingredients, and make it into a paste.
And if you wish to dilute it, do this: one ounce of the remedy, one ounce of wax, one ounce of Bruttian pitch, six ounces of common oil.
Hierocles, a good remedy for recovery.
One must give the horse one ounce of bitter-vetch, for its recovery.
The root, given as a drench, also works.
One must give it gradually, mixed into barley gruel.
We shall give, at first, one handful of chickling-vetch.
By the same author, on what purges.
Myrrh too is among the purging and restorative remedies. Anatolius, on the rearing of foals.
One should not do with horses as with the rearing of other animals, whose young we take away — for this animal is the most affectionate of all.
For after fifteen days we let them graze together with their mothers.
When the foals reach six months, we shall give them soaked barley.
But they should not be separated from the milk either.
But one must be careful to watch for this: that the mares nursing the foals are not covered again.
For, from mating during lactation, the milk spoils, just as with humans too.

Some, wishing to make the hooves harder, heat a potsherd, sprinkle vinegar on it, and place it beneath the hooves; and, once the horses have returned from a journey, wash them with cold water, and apply pig or goat fat with sulphur to the hooves, especially those that have become chafed.
And daily, just as humans enjoy bathing, so too the horse enjoys river water, and even more the sea.
For seawater benefits their bodies more.
You will make the mane and tail glossy by wetting them with wine and oil.
We shall purge the horses with chickpea and bitter-vetch in spring and autumn, and in winter feed them on barley mixed with bitter-vetch.
On the cure of various diseases.
If a horse grows thin, one must give it double the amount of roasted grain and roasted barley, and it must be watered three times a day.
And if it continues to grow thin, bran must be mixed with the grain, and gentle exercise must be used.

And if it does not eat greedily, they strain nightshade and germander leaves through fresh water and pour it into the fodder, and offer soaked bitter-vetch in water, or grind two cyathi of black cummin and mix it with three cups of oil. You will treat those with nausea by mixing a cup of garlic with wine and giving it.
And if it is also seized by difficult urination, egg white mixed with the aforesaid remedies and poured in through the mouth will help. For horses and mules, moist fodder differs from dry.
We shall therefore write out the signs of all the diseases separately, so that even the layman may know them.
And I shall show this from the case of horses and all draught animals.
The first of the diseases is foot-gout.

It occurs first in horses and other draught animals from chilling and from difficult urination, or when it results from exertion or many drives, or when, having grown hot from work, it is suddenly chilled after a journey, or from cold, or from phlegm.
One must therefore recognize the timing of all these and observe whether the draught animal is healthy.
This disease is like bile-sickness in humans, and its signs are these: a mist forms over the head and in the eyes, the eyelids stick together, and it tosses its head and sheds copious tears.

Sometimes the tongue too is cold and pale, and, whichever way it turns, [lacuna], and its ears droop, and it pushes its head downward, and the little veins in its head, full of blood, stand out, and it breathes hot and rapid breath.
These, then, are the signs from the head.

And these are the signs in the body: the loin, the spinal veins, and the sinews become painfully and violently strained, and sweat flows onto the loin, though very little; it butts its head, the tail hangs heavy, and it draws it in.

Sometimes the rectum is also drawn in, sometimes the veins near the rectum throb, and the member does not extend, and it does not want to urinate forward, and its flanks look altered and heave frequently, and its haunches are sore, and they cannot lie down.

And in the legs they become sore, and a tremor remains in each one, and lameness, and it drags itself and cannot stand, but walks on tiptoe. The sinews in the legs are stiffly dry with numbness, and the little veins are full of blood.
One must cut the skin at the groin; and if it does not stop, one must excise the testicles, and it will recover.

Pelagonius's preliminary drink, which makes all animals recover more quickly, cleanses everything internally, and heals; it also works against every affliction and old cough; it also works against consumption, pneumonia-cough, pneumonia, and whatever is diseased.

The preparation is this: half a pint of vetch-gruel with linseed, one raw pig's rectum or a small measure; and if a small measure or a pig's rectum cannot be found, a kid's head with the trotters and the gut.
Add two bundles of hyssop, fifteen bulbs, one bundle of rue, one ounce of fresh bay-berries, thirty dates, three heads of garlic, six ounces of goat fat, one bundle of pennyroyal.
Clean and crush all these together, and boil in cistern water, until the aforesaid meat has completely broken down and only the bones remain.
Add water repeatedly, so that it does not burn dry or make the broth too greasy.
And after this, strain it, and, adding three ounces of tragacanth, portion it out over three days.
Put the tragacanth into warm water one day beforehand, so that it ferments, and add three portions of must-syrup, that is, one each day, six eggs by number for the animal, and rose oil.
Mix all these together, and give it as a preliminary drink to the fasting animal.
Eumelus, for the shoulders.
If blood congests the shoulders, one must open the veins of the legs, and, mixing frankincense meal with the blood, rub down the shoulders against the grain of the hair.
You will stop the flowing veins by applying the animal's own dung.
On the next day, draw blood from the same places again, and, feeding it green fodder, mix about three cyathi of leek juice with oil and pour it into its throat through a horn.
After this, let it be exercised a little, and after six days force it to swim too, and let it gradually take its usual food again.
Hippocrates, on prolapse of the rectum.

If the rectum protrudes from chilling, you will treat it thus: soak the everted rectum with warm water, wine, and oil, then sprinkle on Egyptian alum, or chop bramble and cypress galls and sprinkle those on, and, applying a sponge to the rectum, soak it again with warm vinegar-and-water.

Let it immediately eat tender chaste-tree shoots, and let it eat a few soaked bitter-vetch and drink something warm, and let it be entirely covered with a blanket and stand in a suitably warm place, and let it be drenched with wine and oil, and with celery seed boiled in enough wine.
And if the rectum cannot easily be pushed back in, scarify it sufficiently with a phlebotomy blade, and press on the previously painful place, mixing in alum and oil.

It is dangerous to cut away the fleshy protrusions of the rectum; instead, flush it with mastic-tree leaves, bay, and cypress boiled in wine, and anoint it with the wound-remedy, which is prepared as follows: [lacuna]
You will break up knotty growths in animals in this way: boil two ounces of verdigris, two ounces of chalcitis, three grams of beet, and use, and the growths will disperse.
Another.
Two ounces of chalcitis-flower, one ounce of beet, two ounces of niter, two ounces of silphium-sap, six ounces of sharp vinegar.
For boils.
If a horse has boils, before they come to a head, hold them with three fingers and say: 'I am working on you.'
For pain of the armpits. And if the animal suffers from the windpipe.

If the animal suffers from the windpipe, it will have the same signs as those with difficult breathing: notably the tail becomes stiff, the head droops downward along with the ears, the member hangs slack, the intestines rumble, and the testicles become inflamed.
The cause of such diseases is bile obstructing the passage of blood.
One must therefore open the veins at the back of the neck, and the chest, or the shoulders too, and rub down with the blood, as we said before.

Then take one ounce of tragacanth, grains of pepper; soak the tragacanth for one day, mix everything together, and, grinding it into one cup of old wine, adding honey, insert it through the left nostril for four days, giving four cyathi each day.
And force the animal to walk on a winding road.
Foment the head often with hot water, and continually anoint and rub down the whole body.
Rub the body more vigorously, so that the skin, which has become stuck fast to the bones, softens.
Let it be given the food described for those with difficult breathing, and let its drink be water in which couch-grass and trefoil have been boiled.
For the onset of difficult breathing.
Seven grubs from a bakery, seven cyathi of wine, two cyathi of oil, two eggs; grind them all, warm it, and drench through the nostrils.
Theomnestus, on a case where we suspect that it has suffered some injury from a fall or a cliff.

When a horse or other draught animal falls into a ditch or some pit, and shows no visible wound, but we suspect it has suffered some internal injury, let us help it thus: let us drench it with Cyrenaic sap, about the size of a Pontic walnut, in three cups of wine, pouring it in through the nostrils; or make a dripping lye from oak or holly-oak ash and drench with two cups of the lye and an equal amount of wine; or the juice of red acacia with wine, or of sour pomegranate with wine.
But when, having fallen, it begins to pass loose, wet dung, do not treat it.
For it is beyond saving. On paraplasmata.
Paraplasmata occur from much and strenuous running.
The front fetlocks swell up, so that they seem full of fluid; scarify, then, the pastern-joints and foment them.
If this does not help, do not scrape the swollen place at the scratches with the spatula-probe, so that you do not cause a flux, but only disperse it, and soak the places with vinegar and niter.
The next day, use the soft plaster made with galbanum.
For you will either heal the affected parts completely, or at least relieve them considerably.
To make white hairs turn black.
Chop equal parts of a sweet ingredient, opium, and licorice, take them up with Aminean wine, and, making it honey-like in consistency, anoint.
Hippocrates, on unruly hairs.
If hairs [are unruly, treat] with vinegar, wild pears, wild raisins. On making a horse bald.
Smear on hot crushed vetch all over, or boil turnips and smear them on.
For a horse: grind medicinal oak-gall in vinegar, then, dissolving it, grind myrtle and smear on.
To make a chestnut horse's hairs white.
Grind alum with water and rub it on the hairs, and, taking tanner's sumac and kneading it in vinegar, smear it on, and they will turn white.
To make a horse's white hairs black.

You will make a horse's white hairs black thus: boil in water the thistle that dyers use, and astringe the hairs with it, and, taking either dyer's-vitriol or chalcitis, smear it on, and add blue vitriol to the ointment too. Hippocrates, on chafing.
If chafing occurs in the groin from running or driving, it happens most quickly to pack-animals that are young and spirited.
Treat it, then, by fomenting with warm brine, then applying sponges soaked in a decoction of dog's-foot plant.
And if it persists, poultice it the same way as sprains, then use a soft plaster.
And if it becomes chronic, one must cauterize it in a lattice pattern.
Do the same for chafing near the tail too; or take lard soaked in wine with dried figs,
soaked for several days, and apply this as a poultice.
On stomach trouble and foaming.
If a horse or another draught animal has stomach trouble, it coughs harshly and often, and sometimes brings up foam from within.
This occurs during driving.
[So it sometimes also brings up foam.]
Give such an animal bull's gall with honey. With lard, vetch-cakes made of ground bitter-vetch, and, chopping honey and lard together, give three cups.
Let it abstain from chaff, and meanwhile give it grass.
It works marvelously.
On ileus.
Ileus occurs when it gorges on fodder and does not digest it.
This is the worst of afflictions.
[When it gorges, something like a stone forms in the colon.]
When, then, this affliction occurs, it throws itself down and rises repeatedly and walks about, and again throws itself down and twists onto its back and its flanks, and groans from the constriction.
One must help such an animal thus: one must anoint the hand and insert it into the rectum, and remove the dung lying near it, and rub the bladder gently, so that it urinates.
For it is not, as they say, that the wind twists, but that the passage becomes constricted.
Drench it, then, taking cabbage juice, one cup of oil, one cyathus of celery, and boil with one cup of wine, and, having boiled it, drench, and rub it down with wine and oil,
warm, and force it into the stable, and give it an enema through the rectum with warm wine-and-oil.
Use walks up and down slopes, so that the gases may find their way to pass.
For once the discharge occurs, it will be relieved of the distension.
Put chaff into a sack, soak it with hot water, and bind it under the flanks, and it will reheat, and use fire generally, if possible, quickly.
For this affliction is fatal.
Give it also to eat, if it faints, either oats or green fodder, or dry fodder sprinkled with water.
Give it water, as much as is sufficient.

The animal gives these signs if it is going to recover: if it pricks up its ears and its breathing is steady, and it breathes warm air and passes dung. But if it is not going to recover, these are the signs: the member hangs exposed, cold sweat breaks out on the flanks, the breathing is shallow, the forelegs are stretched out and cold, the neck is stiff, and the nostril is cold.
On pimples.
If you use frankincense with wine, or Cyrenaic sap, or henbane fruit, or wild raisins, you will cure it.
On bruises.
If you wish to remove bruises, put in enough blue vitriol, and, having boiled it in vinegar, use enough of this; or also boil up sulphur, and, having chopped it, boil it in vinegar and smear it on.
On a horse wasting away.
If a horse will not eat though not afflicted by any disease, examine it and you will find the roof of the mouth swollen.
Draw blood, then, from the gums, and rub with salt and marjoram, and, having bound it, let the phlegm drain away.
Then wash out its mouth, and do not give it food for one day.
And if it does not settle, rub the swollen palate with fine salt the next day.
On the neck vertebra.
If the neck and the vertebra become weak, hindering its gait, bleed the joint-veins.
Also apply a small fleece soaked in wine-and-oil, bind it on, and, having tied it up, let it eat.
Hippocrates, if a horse eats hellebore.
If a horse eats white hellebore, vomiting occurs, and it coughs, and develops diarrhea. On a horse's gluttony.
If a horse eats too greedily, mix beans with the barley, and whatever it leaves behind in the manger, remove.
On taming.
If a horse or mule is unruly, take a bronze ring, pierce the parts around the jaw with a hot iron, and fit it there. On hellebore.
If a horse eats it, mix pomegranate juice with brine, or drench with cress fruit and the juice of sour pomegranate with warm water.
Diagnosis of diseases.

If it has collapsed from exhaustion, or is afflicted with barley-surfeit, and sometimes with fever, matching the signs written above, warm the water by itself in a very warm place, and treat it this way, and let it move about under cover.
And if it recovers in strength and vigor, discontinue those remedies, and let it keep to a regular regimen.
Let it be trotted a little, and let it be fumigated if possible, and let straw bedding be laid beneath it.
Lead it around outside, on soft ground, or preferably by a river.

And when it begins to recover, these are the signs: it frisks about when led out. But if none of these remedies has any effect, when it does not respond properly to treatment, cut without delay the veins from its neck—

and then, as though finding it in health, call it out, and, leading it outside, chop up 'pelendryon'; if possible, having ground the barley fine, sprinkle it with water, dissolve the 'pelendryon' in it, and pour it in through the mouth.
And if the horse cannot eat, one must prepare and give it oil-and-honey; warming it with water, or grinding it thoroughly with salt, give it.
On mules.

A mule does not suffer the same afflictions as a horse, whether male or female, but, just as its body is drier and lighter, and its womb-passages are closed up from the dryness of its flesh, so too diseases pass over it more easily.

For the male and female mule, then, limiting the treatment as it applies externally to the genitals, and, for shoulder-joint troubles and lamenesses, prepare all of them according to the same principle, and rely on incisions and dry remedies.
The onset of these diseases, then, is recognized, as has indeed been written above.
Whenever a mule's hips become dislocated, its womb-passages are pulled out of place, with abrasions and much bleeding.
Lay her down, and, rubbing the hips, and, reaching down beneath the scales, behind, under the hip, and beside the tail, immediately rub away the dark matter from the body.
Then rub in fine salt with one cup of dark wine, and blow it into the nostrils, and, grinding in eggs, you will calm its distress.
Furthermore, wash the head thoroughly with a cup of dark wine and plenty of hot water, then the whole body, starting from the head.
And if some other part of the body is lame, apply none of the incisions described earlier for the horse's own case, and do not apply cauteries, if it lies stretched out.
But if it needs an incision, cauterize with two strokes on the neck, on each side.

For other ailments, use the same remedy as a drench, and, anointing the body, foment it, and pour in one cup of fragrant dark wine, and, straining it through linen, pour it into the mouth this way, and it will recover.
Hippocrates: an aromatic remedy for cattle.
Three ounces each of costus and centaury, one ounce of wormwood, iris, common celery, and saffron-sediment, equal amounts. [The manuscript breaks off here, unfinished.]
